newsitem.title: CUBA: Baseball-Cuba cancels baseball with U.S. after explosions.
newsitem.headline: Baseball-Cuba cancels baseball with U.S. after explosions.

text.p: Cuba withdrew at the last minute on Monday from a series of baseball games against the United States, citing fears for the safety of players and saying one reason for the cancellation was the weekend bombing of two Havana hotels.
A statement by the Cuban national sports body INDER said it decided conditions for the eight-game series -- due to start in Norwich, Connecticut, on Tuesday -- were "not favourable for our team."
Two small bombs exploded within minutes of each other on Saturday in the lobbies of the Hotel Nacional and Hotel Capri, slightly injuring three people and causing damage to windows and furniture.
A brief Interior Ministry statement said the ministry had evidence to show the people responsible for the bombs and the material used were from the United States. The ministry gave no other details.

But official suspicion was likely to fall on hardline groups among the Cuban exile community in Miami opposed to President Fidel Castro's communist government. Some of these groups have carried out violent action in the past, or have threatened to do so.

The director of the U.S. baseball squad, Mike Fiore, said the news of the Cuban cancellation was a "heavy blow." He said the U.S. Baseball Federation stood to lose some $75,000 to $100,000 because of the cancellation.
The baseball series between the United States and Cuba has been held annually for more than a decade.

Cuba's Olympic Committee President, Jose Ramon Fernandez, told the Cuban news agency Prensa Latina that Cuba believed action by exiles such as insults and attempts to get Cuban players to defect would be worse than usual if they travelled at this time.

Fernandez said U.S. sporting authorities and sports people were not involved in what he called the campaign against Cuban athletes. But there was failure by organisers of some competitions and by local officials in some U.S. towns to ensure a proper climate for sports, he said.

The INDER statement said the Saturday bombings added to other issues, including reported plans by hardline Cuban exile groups, which it termed "the Miami counter-revolutionary mafia," to harass the Cuban team during the series.
The statement also cited the "constant provocations" that the national squad has been subjected to in the United States.
In the last six years, several Cuban star players have defected to the United States, to the dismay of authorities.

They include pitchers Osvaldo Fernandez and Rene Arocha, both with the San Francisco Giants, Livan Hernandez with the Florida Marlins, Rolando Arrojo with Tampa, and shortstop Rey Ordonez with the New York Mets.
The INDER statement did not mention these cases.

But it said that during past visits the Cuban baseball squad had suffered "threatening phone calls, offers of gifts so they defect, and the actual presence in those places (team hotels) of people who knock on the door of players' rooms making the same proposals to them."
The United States and Cuba have no diplomatic relations and have been politically hostile since the 1959 revolution that brought Castro to power. Sports exchanges are permitted.
